app.title: ExoPlanet AI | Kepler CNN Detector
app.summary: A person enters a star's catalogue number, or picks a demo star, and runs a pipeline that downloads the star's archived light curve, picks one fixed-length window from it and scores that window with a trained convolutional network. The interface reports whether the score clears a calibrated threshold and which confidence tier it falls in, with the action each tier calls for. If the person supplies an orbital period, it phase-folds the light curve to check for a secondary eclipse and flags the star as a likely eclipsing binary. The full light curve, the scored window and the dips it contains are plotted, and a separate page sets the result against the model's validated performance and known limits.

task.text: Screen one star's light curve for a transit-like signal with a trained classifier, and vet a candidate against the most common false positive.

data.text: Archived photometric time series for single stars, fetched by catalogue ID and stitched across observing quarters, plus an optional orbital period.
data.item: one star's light curve (brightness over time)

stage.text: screening archived light curves for planet candidates, before follow-up

mechanism.text: An input form (ID, demo picker, auto-filled period) starts a staged pipeline whose progress is shown step by step; its outputs fill a verdict box with score and tier, an eclipsing-binary check panel, and two linked line charts in which the scored window is shaded on the full series and repeated close up. Sidebar navigation switches to a performance dashboard of tables, curves and a tabbed results gallery.

field.text: transit photometry classified with a 1D convolutional network, in astronomy

workflow.name: score one item with a trained classifier and vet the call against a known false positive

steps.here: Type a catalogue number or pick a demo star, then Run downloads quarters 1–8 of long-cadence flux from the public archive, median-normalises each quarter and stitches them, with progress shown and results cached.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: The light curve is gap-filled, median-subtracted, cut to the highest-variance fixed-length window, normalised and smoothed, then scored 0–1 by the network.

steps.step: classify the item against a threshold and place it in a tier
steps.here: A calibrated threshold gives 'planet candidate' or 'no planet'; a HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW badge points at the tier guide's recommended action, and low scores get a warning naming likely causes.

steps.step: check the call against a known false-positive cause
steps.here: With a period entered (auto-filled for known stars, 0 to skip), the curve is phase-folded, primary and secondary eclipse depths are measured above noise gates, and a secondary/primary ratio over one half flags an eclipsing binary; a doubled-period fold catches equal eclipses.
The full light curve is drawn faintly with the scored window shaded and overlaid, dips below −2σ marked, and the preprocessed window the network saw drawn on its own.

steps.step: set the result against the method's validated performance
steps.here: A Performance page shows a results table by evaluation round, ROC curves, score distributions with the threshold, detection rate by signal-to-noise tier, a tabbed figure gallery and a list of known limitations.

distinctive: the classifier sees only one fixed-length window, chosen as the highest-variance stretch, and the chart shades that window on the full series so the person can see what was actually scored

vetting is a period-folding test: the depth of a secondary eclipse relative to the primary, gated against out-of-transit scatter, separates eclipsing binaries from planets, with a doubled-period fallback for equal eclipses
the orbital period is auto-filled from a built-in table for known targets and the vetting step is skipped when it is left at zero
a calibrated detection threshold sits alongside separate confidence tiers, each with a recommended follow-up action, and below-threshold results come with an explanation of likely failure modes
